answer: The retained passages support that cryptocurrency can be property held on trust, but whether a particular customer has a beneficial interest depends on the applicable terms, consent and objectively assessed relationship. The 2023 court rejected trusts under the 2018 terms while preserving the Non-Consenting Customer exception. The 2025 passages distinguish NCC pooled beneficial interests, ETD breach-of-trust claims and Samara’s unsecured claim. These conclusions do not establish a Product Provider’s ownership arrangements or fulfillment of paragraph 10 of 26EC22. Transfer requires an applicable legal principle, materially comparable relationships and actual evidence. Subsequent treatment and the inconsistent treatment of scenario seven remain unresolved.

claims.inference: The distinction is between property capable of being trust property and a trust actually created in the particular relationship. Capability alone does not establish customers’ beneficial ownership.
missing_premises: The terms governing the particular customer and evidence of acceptance or non-consent.

claims.proposition: The 2023 judgment recognizes cryptocurrency as property capable of trust but rejects a trust under the applicable 2018 terms, preserving the NCC exception.
claims.status: Supported by retained judicial conclusion; application remains conditional.

support.quote: Cryptocurrency is “property” and is capable of being held on trust

claims.inference: The 2023 reasons quote principles attributed to Briggs J in Re Lehman Brothers. They support examining the substantive relationship rather than treating labels or agency status as conclusive; their quotation should not be represented as a newly established universal Gatecoin rule.
missing_premises: The complete agreement, governing law and objective circumstances of the target relationship.
A checked account of the quoted principles’ adoption and scope in the full reasons.
claims.proposition: Ownership and trust labels, and even an agency relationship, do not alone determine beneficial ownership.
claims.status: Supported by principles quoted in the retained reasons.

support.quote: The words used by the parties such as ‘trust’, ‘custody’, ‘belonging’, ‘ownership’, ‘title’, may be persuasive, but they are not conclusive in favour of the recognition of B’s proprietary interest in the property, if the terms of the agreement or relationship, viewed objectively, compel a different conclusion.
The identification of a relationship in which A is B’s agent or broker is not conclusive of a conclusion that A is, in relation to the property, B’s trustee
